statement: Using the digits 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, with no digit used more than once, how many even three-digit numbers can be made? (A number cannot start with 0.)

choices.misconception: I forgot that 0 is even, so I only let the number end in 2 or 4.
I chose the even last digit in 3 ways, then gave the first digit 4 choices and the middle 3, forgetting that the first digit cannot be 0: $3 \times 4 \times 3 = 36$.
I counted all the three-digit numbers with different digits, $4 \times 4 \times 3 = 48$, and forgot they must be even.
I only counted the numbers ending in 0 and forgot that 2 and 4 are even too.

hints: Fill the most restricted place first. Which digit is special here?
The last digit must be even and the first digit cannot be 0, and the digit 0 affects both rules. Split into two cases: the number ends in 0, or it ends in 2 or 4.
Ending in 0: $4 \times 3$ numbers. Ending in 2 or 4: the first digit can be neither 0 nor the last digit, which leaves 3 choices.

solutions.reliable: Case 1, last digit 0: the first digit is any of 1, 2, 3, 4 (4 ways) and the middle is any of the 3 digits left, so 12 numbers. Case 2, last digit 2 or 4 (2 ways): the first digit cannot be 0 or the last digit, so 3 ways, and the middle can be any of the 3 digits left, including 0, so $2 \times 3 \times 3 = 18$ numbers. Total 12 + 18 = 30. The transferable idea: when one digit is involved in two restrictions, split into cases on that digit.
solutions.elegant: Count the opposite: there are $4 \times 4 \times 3 = 48$ three-digit numbers with different digits. The odd ones end in 1 or 3 (2 ways), then the first digit has 3 choices (not 0 and not the last digit) and the middle 3, giving 18. So 48 - 18 = 30 are even.

whyOnTest: Tests counting with two restrictions that share the digit 0, where the multiplication principle only works after splitting into cases.
